第 84 章 Three Ways to Be the Manager Your Report Needs成为下属需要的经理的三种方式

Duretti Hirpa / 杜雷蒂·希尔帕

— 第 229 页 —

I've worked as a software developer my whole career—and I've worked everywhere from small mom-and-pop shops, to agencies, to companies going through hypergrowth. At one company, I had a new manager every quarter. Having a slew of managers in a short timeframe trained my eye: I can spot a s--- manager in fewer than three one-on-ones, and I know what the decent ones try to do. I've become obsessed with quickly and accurately unveiling a bad manager and identifying which traits separate the bad ones from the good ones. Let me tell you what I know.

我整个职业生涯都做软件开发者——从夫妻店到代理商到经历超增长的公司都做过。在一家公司，我每季度换一个新经理。短时间内有一堆经理训练了我的眼睛：我能在三次一对一内认出一个烂经理，我知道像样的经理试图做什么。我变得痴迷于快速准确地揭露坏经理、识别哪些特质把坏的和好的分开。让我告诉你我知道什么。

Lesson One: One-on-Ones第一课：一对一

As a manager, you've probably heard that the one-on-one (the weekly meeting where you spend between 30 minutes to an hour with your report) is sacrosanct. A good manager knows this; a great manager lives this. Bad managers leave you waiting in the agreed upon room, eventually messaging some flavor of, "oh, did you need the 1:1 this week?" If your report (like me) has been socialized to be agreeable and consents to skipping, you will have set a dangerous precedent. This is the first fracture.

作为经理，你可能听说过一对一（每周和下属花 30 分钟到一小时的会议）是神圣不可侵犯的。好经理知道这个；伟大经理活出这个。坏经理让你在约定的房间等，最后发消息说「哦，你这周需要一对一吗？」如果你的下属（像我）被社会化得顺从、同意跳过，你就树立了一个危险的先例。这是第一道裂缝。

It's possible that you might not know why skipping a one-on-one is important, so let me tell it to you from one of your own. Marc Hedlund, former vice president of engineering at Etsy and Stripe, says, "Regular one-on-ones are like oil changes; if you skip them, plan to get stranded on the side of the highway at the worst possible time." A one-on-one is an investment in the future. It's a seed you plant, it's regular exercise, it's eight hours of sleep a night.

你可能不知道为什么跳过一对一很重要，让我从你的一个下属角度告诉你。Marc Hedlund，Etsy 和 Stripe 前工程 VP，说：「定期一对一就像换机油；如果你跳过，准备好在最糟糕的时候被困在高速路边。」一对一是对未来的投资。它是你种下的种子，是定期锻炼，是每晚八小时睡眠。

— 第 230 页 —

If you ask to skip, you're sending a message. You're saying to your report, "You're not important to me this week." Like most subversive things that become easier the more you do it, skipping one-on-ones goes from, "You're not important to me this week," to, "You're not important to me," to, "You're not important." Don't do this. Your one-on-ones should be so regular that if one is canceled, your report thinks something happened to you.

如果你要求跳过，你在发一个信息。你在对下属说：「你这周对我不重要。」像大多数你越做越容易的颠覆性事情一样，跳过一对一从「你这周对我不重要」变成「你对我不重要」变成「你不重要」。不要这样做。你的一对一应该如此规律，如果一个被取消，你的下属会觉得你出了什么事。

Lesson Two: Follow Through第二课：贯彻到底

The most helpful advice I can give anyone (and it works in a variety of contexts) is to follow through. What is trust if not consistency over time? Be consistent, show up. Show up physically to your one-on-ones. But, more crucial, show up for your report. Did they ask you a question? Great, that's an assignment. Go find out what you can tell them. If you can't tell them anything, that's fine—but close the loop. Otherwise, you're unreliable; a black hole where my requests go to die. For you to do your job well, I need to trust you. With each successful closing of a loop, you build trust with me, your report. Every closed loop you miss? You teach me that you're not someone I can rely on, and with enough time, I'll treat you accordingly.

我能给任何人的最有用建议（在各种场景都有效）是贯彻到底。信任如果不是随时间的一致性那是什么？保持一致，出现。身体上出现在一对一。但更关键的是，为你的下属出现。他们问了你一个问题吗？好，那是一个任务。去找出你能告诉他们什么。如果你不能告诉他们什么，那也没关系——但闭环。否则你不可靠；我的请求死掉的黑洞。要你做好工作，我需要信任你。每成功闭一个环，你和我、你的下属建立信任。你错过的每个闭环？你教我你不是我可以依靠的人，时间久了我会相应对待你。

Lesson Three: Avoid Causing Anxiety第三课：避免造成焦虑

As your report, I'm intensely aware of you. I'm lurking on your calendar, I'm noticing how and where you spend your time, what you're doing, and with who. I'm talking to your other reports about you. We strategize. That's why when you deviate from your pattern, we'll know. If you ask us whether we have time to chat or if a calendar event shows up with no context, we'll worry (honestly? we think we're getting fired—no matter our standing in the company). Forgetting to set context strikes anxiety into the hearts of your reports—and you're not heartless, are you? Hopefully not, else you wouldn't have chosen a profession trafficking in other people's careers. Remember: you control our careers and our financial prospects. A bad manager forgets this. A good one never does.

作为你的下属，我极度注意你。我潜伏在你的日历上，我注意你怎么和在哪里花时间、你在做什么、和谁。我在和你的其他下属谈论你。我们策略。所以当你偏离模式时我们会知道。如果你问我们有没有时间聊聊，或者一个日历事件没上下文就出现，我们会担心（老实说？我们以为自己要被炒了——不管在公司地位如何）。忘记设上下文把焦虑打进下属心里——你不是没心没肺吧？希望不是，否则你不会选择一个处理别人职业的职业。记住：你控制我们的职业和财务前景。坏经理忘了这个。好经理永远不会。

Caring is what separates a good manager from a bad one. I get it: life is easier when you don't care, when you don't put in the effort. But, if you're going to do this job, and do it well? Caring is the baseline. Being a great manager is not about amassing influence or power or authority. It's about showing up, daily, in small steady ways. When you build up your reports, you enable them to build, too. That's what they'll remember; not the specifics of every project, but the way you, their manager, cared about them. That's something that'll last longer than any tenure at any company. We can build so much more than software when we care.

关心把好经理和坏经理分开。我懂：不关心、不付出努力时生活更容易。但如果你要做这份工作、做好？关心是基线。做伟大经理不是积累影响力或权力或权威。而是每天以小而稳的方式出现。当你培养下属时，你也让他们能培养。那是他们会记住的；不是每个项目的细节，而是你——他们的经理——关心他们的方式。那比任何公司的任何任期都持久。当我们关心时，我们能建的远不止软件。
